## Course Description

HPM 883 is an advanced graduate-level course designed to equip PhD students in Health Policy and Management with sophisticated quantitative research skills. This course is the third installment in the quantitative methods sequence, building on foundations from HPM 881 and HPM 882.

The course integrates experimental design principles with modern causal machine learning methods, following a three-layer framework: **Identification → Estimation → Decision**.

**Core Narrative:** "Does it work?" → "For whom?" → "What should we do?"

**Focus Areas:**

-   Experimental design and randomization inference
-   Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML)
-   Heterogeneous treatment effects and causal forests
-   Policy learning and optimal treatment rules
-   Adaptive experiments and dynamic treatment decisions

**Course Format:** This is a hybrid course combining in-person lectures (theory and discussion) with remote Zoom sessions (coding labs and implementation).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

| \# | Learning Objective | Assessment Evidence |
|--------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | **Design** randomized experiments with appropriate power analysis, randomization strategies, and variance reduction techniques | Labs, Jigsaw, Capstone Project |
| 2 | **Implement** Double/Debiased Machine Learning and doubly-robust estimators for causal inference | Labs, Jigsaw, Capstone Project |
| 3 | **Estimate** heterogeneous treatment effects using causal forests and meta-learners | Labs, Jigsaw, Capstone Project |
| 4 | **Evaluate** Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimates using calibration diagnostics | Labs, Capstone Project |
| 5 | **Learn** optimal treatment policies using policy trees and off-policy evaluation | Labs, Capstone Project |
| 6 | **Understand** adaptive experiments including bandits and Thompson sampling | Jigsaw, Capstone Project |
| 7 | **Diagnose** common problems including overlap violations, confounding, and model misspecification | Labs, Jigsaw, Capstone Project |
| 8 | **Produce** reproducible research using modern workflow tools (Git, Quarto, Codespaces) | Lab 0, All Labs, Capstone Project |

## Required Materials

### Textbooks (Both FREE Online)

1.  **Chernozhukov, V., Hansen, C., Kallus, N., Spindler, M., & Syrgkanis, V. (2025)** *Applied Causal Inference Powered by ML and AI* Available free at: [causalml-book.org](https://causalml-book.org/)

2.  **Wager, S. (2024)** *Causal Inference: A Statistical Learning Approach* Available free at: [Stanford PDF](http://web.stanford.edu/~swager/causal_inf_book.pdf)

### Software

-   **R** (version 4.3 or higher)
-   **RStudio** or **Positron** IDE
-   **Key R Packages:** tidyverse, renv, targets, DeclareDesign, estimatr, DoubleML, grf, policytree, did, Synth, cobalt, WeightIt

All software is free and open-source. See [Setup Guide](Resources/setup-guide.qmd) for installation instructions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Course Structure

The course is organized into 6 units over 14 weeks, following the core narrative arc:

| Unit | Topic | Weeks | Core Question |
|----|----|----|----|
| 0 | Foundations: Potential Outcomes & DAGs | 1 | Setup |
| 1 | Experimental Design & Randomization | 2-3 | Does it work? |
| 2 | Double/Debiased Machine Learning | 4-6 | Does it work? |
| 3 | HTE & Causal Forests | 7-8 | For whom? |
| 4 | Policy Learning | 9 | What should we do? (static) |
| 5 | Adaptive Experiments | 10-11 | What should we do? (dynamic) |
| — | Capstone & Presentations | 12-14 | Integration |

## Assessment & Grading

### Grade Composition

| Component            | Weight   | Description                  |
|----------------------|----------|------------------------------|
| Labs                 | 30%      | 4 required labs              |
| Jigsaw Participation | 20%      | \~5 sessions (one per unit)  |
| Capstone Project     | 45%      | Paper + code + presentation  |
| Peer Review          | 5%       | Review of one peer's project |
| **Total**            | **100%** |                              |


### Grading Scale

Final course grades follow the [UNC Graduate School grading scale](https://handbook.unc.edu/grading.html):

-   **H** — High Pass (93-100): Clear excellence
-   **P** — Pass (80-92): Entirely satisfactory graduate work
-   **L** — Low Pass (70-79): Inadequate graduate work
-   **F** — Fail (0-69)

## Policies

### Communication

**Course Questions:** Please use the [Canvas Discussion Board](https://uncch.instructure.com/courses/108894/discussion_topics) to ask questions about problem sets, exercises, and other class materials. This ensures everyone benefits from the answers. If you email me or the TA a question that is not personal in nature, we will ask you to post it to Canvas instead.

::: callout-tip
## Participation Bonus

If you are "on the bubble" for your final grade, your participation in helping answer classmates' questions on the discussion board will be carefully considered!
:::

**Announcements:** We use Canvas/email for time-critical announcements. For updates on class materials, check the [course website](https://hpm883.ssylvia.io) (NOT Canvas) regularly — there will be adjustments as we go through the semester.

**Anonymous Feedback:** I am continuously trying to improve the course. Please share feedback anytime via the [anonymous feedback form](https://unc.az1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_b3O2k8IV6hVLn9k) — don't be shy!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Attendance

-   Attendance is **not** formally taken, but participation in jigsaw activities will be recorded
-   You do **not** need to email the instructor or TA if you will be absent
-   For jigsaw discussions, you may drop your **lowest 2** session scores
-   When possible, class recordings will be provided
-   For sessions marked as **in-person**, there will not be a live Zoom option for remote attendance

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### AI Use Policy

The use of AI tools (such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, or Claude) is **permitted and encouraged** for:

-   Debugging code
-   Understanding error messages
-   Learning syntax and package functions
-   Generating code snippets for adaptation

However, you are responsible for all code you submit — AI-generated code must be understood, tested, and verified. Conceptual understanding cannot be outsourced.

**Required Disclosure:** For any assignment, you must include a brief note indicating which AI model(s) you used and how. For example: "Used Claude 3.5 to help debug the bootstrap function" or "Used GitHub Copilot for code completion throughout."

### Labs & Problem Sets

Labs are intentionally challenging and combine theoretical and empirical (coding) components.

**Submission Requirements:**

-   Submit both a **PDF report** and the **code** used to generate results via GitHub Classroom
-   Late submissions will **not** be accepted
-   You may use either **R or Python** (Stata and other pre-packaged solutions beyond the basics are not permitted)

**Collaboration Policy:**

I encourage you to work in groups and discuss approaches. However, you must do your own work — I do not want to receive multiple copies of the exact same submission.

### Late Work (Capstone Only)

-   Late submissions: -10% per 24 hours
-   After 48 hours: No credit without prior arrangement
-   Extensions may be granted for documented circumstances if requested before the deadline
